title: "Hardcoded Version vs Dependency Management"
tagline: "Or what to do when one hardcoded version overrides everything else"

#### ! Scenario

*Or what to do when one hardcoded version overrides everything else*
This scenario shows what happens when a version defined in a BOM (`<dependencyManagement>`) and a version explicitly declared in `<dependencies>` disagree.

::: {.callout-note title="Tool Versions"}
This scenario was tested with **Maven 3.9**; the behaviour shown applies to Maven 3.x.
:::

#### ! Example

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4.4
graph LR
    Root[Project Root] -- imports --> BOM[demo-bom:1.0.0]
    Root --> LibA[lib-a:2.0.0]
    Root --> LibB[lib-b]
    BOM -. suggests .-> LibA_BOM[lib-a:1.0.0]
    BOM -. suggests .-> LibB_BOM[lib-b:1.0.0]
```

```{.xml include="pom.xml" snippet="s4-deps"}
```

#### ! Expect
Explicitly declared versions win over managed suggestions.

#### ! Actual
They do. `lib-a` resolves to `2.0.0`; `lib-b`, declared without a version, takes the BOM's `1.0.0`.

#### ! Why
For the project's own direct dependencies, `<dependencies>` is the final authority and `<dependencyManagement>` only fills in what is missing. The managed version still governs `lib-a`'s *transitives*, which is why `lib-b` (requested by nothing at `2.0.0` here, but managed at `1.0.0`) stays put. Note the contrast with Gradle, where a plain `platform()` constraint and a direct declaration compete on version number rather than rank ([GS4](../../gradle-demo/scenario-4-override/guide.qmd)).

#### ! Fix
*   **If the override was accidental:** delete the `<version>` so the BOM is back in control.
*   **If the override is deliberate** (a patched release, a bug fix the BOM has not caught up with): keep it, add a comment saying why and when it can be removed, and test the libraries that depend on it.
*   **If you want to stop overrides happening at all:** Maven has no `enforcedPlatform`. Use the Enforcer Plugin's `dependencyConvergence` or `bannedDependencies` rules to fail the build when a direct version drifts from the managed one.

#### ! Risk
* LOW Overriding to a patch release the BOM maintainers will ship next week.
* MEDIUM Overriding a library the BOM's other artifacts depend on; they were tested against the managed version, not yours.
* HIGH Leaving an override in place after the BOM has caught up. You are now pinned to a version nobody is testing.

#### ! Control
Be careful when overriding BOMs. You might break compatibility with other libraries managed by that BOM. If you must override, ensure you test thoroughly and record the reason in the POM.

#### ! Check

`mvn dependency:tree`

**What to look for:** The explicitly declared version in the tree (`lib-a:jar:2.0.0`) rather than the BOM's version.

**Conclusion:** A version written directly in `<dependencies>` always overrides `<dependencyManagement>` for that declaration.

#### ! Scales
Overriding BOMs is common when patching a vulnerability before the BOM maintainers release an update.

#### ! Takeaway
A direct version always beats a managed one. That makes targeted overrides easy and silent drift from the BOM just as easy.

#### ! Wild

A common pattern with the [Spring Boot BOM](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/appendix/dependency-versions/index.html) is needing a patched library version before the next Boot release bundles it. For example, when Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) hit, teams couldn't wait for a coordinated Spring Boot update; they declared the patched `log4j-core` version directly in `<dependencies>`, overriding the BOM's managed version. Spring's own [documentation](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/how-to/build.html#howto.build.customize-dependency-versions) describes this as the intended escape hatch: a direct `<dependency>` declaration always takes precedence over `<dependencyManagement>`.
